text: Kashmiri cuisine refers to the traditional culinary practices of the Kashmiri people, with rice serving as a staple food since ancient times. The equivalent of "bread and butter" in Kashmiri is haakh-batte, meaning greens and rice. The cuisine is generally meat-heavy, with the region having the highest per capita consumption of mutton in the subcontinent. In most Kashmiri meals, bread is not included; it is typically consumed only with tea in the morning, afternoon, and evening. Cooking methods for vegetables, mutton, homemade cheese (paneer), and legumes are similar among Muslims and Pandits, except that Muslims use onions, garlic, and shallots instead of asafoetida. Lamb or sheep is preferred, though beef is also popular. Cockscomb flower, known as "mawal" in Kashmiri, is boiled to produce a red food coloring used in certain dishes, especially in Wazwan. Pandit cuisine uses Kashmiri red chili powder and ratanjot for color in dishes like rogan josh, while Kashmiri Muslim cuisine uses chilies in moderate amounts and avoids hot dishes at large meals. Vegetable curries are common, and meat is traditionally considered an expensive indulgence. Wazwan dishes, beyond weddings, are prepared on special occasions like Eids, alongside rice, vegetables, and salad. Iconic dishes such as Rogan Josh, Gushtaba, Yakhni, and Kahwa have gained global recognition and are featured in gourmet menus worldwide, with increasing visibility in food festivals in London and Dubai and fine-dining experiences in New York and Toronto. In India, upscale Kashmiri restaurants have opened in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad, often run by members of the Kashmiri community or curated by chefs specializing in Wazwan, helping preserve and promote the region’s gastronomic heritage. This growth is supported by food influencers, YouTube chefs, and curated pop-up events. The cultural and culinary roots of Kashmiri cuisine are linked to South Asia, Persian, and Central Asian cuisines, shaped by historical interactions. The term kabab is Arabic, korma has Turkish roots, and rogan josh, yakhaen, ab gosht, riste, and goshtabh originate from Persian sources. A legend states that the Kashmir valley was once a vast mountain lake, and soil layers contain remains of freshwater fish, fossil oysters, and water chestnut shells at 457 meters above the valley. Snake and fire worship from Iran began to influence Kashmir from Paleolithic times, with serpents buried with insects and grains splashed at shrines. The Bommai Sopore archaeological site, discovered in 2005, features the first prehistoric rock engraving in Kashmir, depicting chase and game scenes. Recent excavations in Overa valley, Pahalgam, have revealed Paleolithic stone tools, including single-edged blades for hunting. Even before the Megalithic culture, there is evidence of wheat, barley, and lentil cultivation. Clear agricultural evidence, including large grain storages and rachises of wheat and barley, dates back to 2500 BC at Qasim Bagh. The Kashmir Valley contains multiple Northern Neolithic sites, possibly as early as 3000 BC, with evidence of broom-corn millet movement across Inner Asian mountains. Lentil samples from Pethpuran Teng date to around 2700 BC, one of the earliest pulse crops in the region. The valley’s lower latitude allowed crop cultivation without the need for traits found in higher latitudes. At Burzahom, stone hearths, ceramic structures, rectangular harvesters with curved edges, and harpoons indicate hunting, fishing, and cultivation. Artistic depictions include a hunting scene with a dog and sun path diagram. Mortar and pestles made of volcanic rock are similar to those used today. The presence of lentils indicates contact with Central Asia, and harvesters with two holes suggest contact with China. At Gufkral, settlers engaged in wild game and domesticated animals such as wild sheep, goat, cattle, red deer, wolf, Himalayan ibex, and bear. Roasting occurred outside dwellings, and tools like piercers and scrapers were used for flesh preparation. In Phase IB, cattle and common peas were introduced, and pigs and fish appeared in the late Neolithic. Bones of hare, hedgehog, rodents, and beaver were also found. Emmer wheat at Kanispur suggests Harappan contact with Neolithic Kashmir. With the Aryan migration around the 8th century BC, fire worship became embedded in Kashmiri culture, including the practice of a phallic emblem of cooked rice. The local ceremony of vayuk resembles the Iranian Farvadin, where on a special day, Kashmiri Muslims visit graves and distribute rice loaves. Earthen thalis and handis have been found from the Indo-Greek period (200 BC–1st century AD) and later in Harwan, Kanispur, and Semthan. Kushan coins, especially those of Kanishka, show a motif of a king sacrificing at an altar. The Kushan period features a double-cropping pattern, indicating agricultural change after a post-Neolithic decline. Horticultural and foraging items such as Vitis vinifera, Emblica officinalis, Ziziphus nummularia, Juglans regia, and Prunus amygdalus were part of the diet. At Kanispur, barley dominates, while at Semthan, wheat is more common. Kashmir had trade links with Rome via Gilgit and Yasin valley, exporting saffron and dolomiaea costus (kutha), which was used in Rome for food scenting and wine seasoning. Military contacts existed between the Karkota kingdom and the Tang Dynasty, with Kashmir supplying agricultural goods to Chinese troops in Gilgit in 722 AD. Islam arrived in Kashmir through mixed Iranian and Central Asian influences, and Kashmiri Hindus practiced vegetarianism, avoided garlic and onions, and had practices that would have alarmed orthodox Hindus, such as drinking water brought by Muslims and eating food cooked in Muslim boats. The rishi cult, associated with Hinduism, emphasized vegetarianism, non-injury to animals, and avoidance of garlic and onions. Nund Rishi is said to have eaten dried dandelion leaves, and Lal Ded practiced strict vegetarianism. When Yusuf Shah Chak signed a treaty with Akbar in 1586, one condition was that the mint, saffron, and game would remain under imperial control. In Srinagar, poor people’s meals included ghee, milk, beef, onions, wine, pickles, and vinegar. During the Mughal era, rice, fish, and vegetables were staples, and butter and fats were avoided due to the cold climate. River water was not drunk in South Kashmir; instead, people consumed warm Dal Lake water. In 1635–36, a conflict arose between Shias and Sunnis over mulberry consumption at Maisuma, and in 1641, unprecedented floods and famine devastated villages. Shahjahan sent 30,000 rupees to Tarbiyat Khan to aid the poor and established five food centers. Cow slaughter was punishable by death, with many accused individuals publicly hanged. Rulers’ short-sighted policies led to an agrarian crisis, with Sikh rulers imposing half of paddy production as government share. The population dropped from 800,000 in 1822–1823 to 120,000 in 1835. Coarse rice and haakh were the main foods, with wheat and maize serving as staples in areas with poor irrigation. Aquatic products like singhara (water nuts) were consumed in certain regions. Kashmiri apples were transported over 12 days by coolies to Rawalpindi. The 1878–79 famine was deadly, and during Maharaja Ranbir Singh’s reign, fishing by men was made illegal. Those who killed cows were boiled in oil and hung publicly. Villagers had no right to waste land, only to plant trees, which they owned. Officials often took milk and butter from gujjars without payment. Ancient Kashmiri scriptures and travelers' accounts mention foods including chicken, fish, game, and other items. Apart from chicken, fish, and game, Kashmiris use only mutton or goat meat. Over 75% of sheep are cross-breeds known as Kashmir Merino, providing both meat and wool. Bakkarwal goats belong to the rare Kaghani breed, prized for meat. Beef is consumed in towns and villages, especially for affordability. In some villages, beef-eaters are separated from mutton-eaters during wazwan feasts. A class divide exists between those who eat kat maaz (mutton), considered elite, and those who eat bad maaz (beef), considered lower-class. The largest rabbit breeding farm in North India is located in Wussan village, Baramulla, and rabbit meat is increasingly consumed as a lean, nutritious alternative, especially by people with cardiac issues. The Kashmir Aenz is the only recognized domestic goose breed in India, with rearing dating back to ancient times, as noted by Sir Walter R. Lawrence. In Srinagar, geese are sold in Batmaloo and Lal Chowk, and affluent families make geese pickles for winter. The Duke of Bedford sent 10,000 trout eggs in 1899, which perished, but a second consignment from Scotland in 1899 succeeded. Rainbow and brown trout adapted well, while indigenous snow trout (known as alegaad) thrives in both standing and flowing water. There were 137 private fish farms in Anantnag, declared the 'Trout District of India'. Poultry farms follow European standards, with free-range eggs produced using permaculture and no-dig gardening. Chick varieties like Kalinga brown, Vanraja, and Kashmir Commercial Layer are collected for organic brown eggs. The Kashmir Duck (batook) is reared across districts, with the highest population in Bandipora, followed by Kupwara, Baramulla, Srinagar, and others. Kashmir duck eggs are white or green-shelled and average 66.20 grams. Kalij pheasant (wan kokur) lays 6 to 10 eggs per clutch and is served soft-boiled in olive-green shells with a sprinkle of celery salt and buttered soldiers. Kashmiri rice varieties include Mushk Budji, grown in higher reaches, which received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in February 2022. Kashmiri red rice, known as Zaag Batt, is grown in Tangdhar near the Pakistan border and valued for its texture and taste. In 2009, farmers in the region harvested Basmati rice for the first time. The most commonly used Kashmiri vegetables are haakh (collard greens or kale), monj haak (kohlrabi), tsochael (mallow), bamchoont (quince), kral mound (shepherds purse), saze posh (holly hock), and nadur (lotus stem).

People in Kashmir consume a variety of rice, including the nutty and fragrant Mushk Budji, grown in the higher reaches of the Kashmir Valley, which received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in February 2022. This rice is noted for its harmonious blend of taste, aroma, and rich organoleptic properties. Kashmiri red rice, known locally as Zaag Batt, is cultivated in the village of Tangdhar on the border with Pakistan and is valued for its superior texture and taste. In 2009, farmers in the region harvested Basmati rice for the first time. The most commonly used Kashmiri vegetables include haakh (collard greens or kale), monj Haak (kohlrabi), tsochael (mallow), bamchoont (quince), kral mound (shepherds purse), saze posh (holly hock), nadur (lotus stem), praan (shallots), aubuj (sorrel), mawal (cockscomb), wushkofur (camphor), tila gogul (mustard), and gor (water-chestnut). The floating vegetable garden on Dal Lake is the second largest wholesale market in the world, where men of all ages trade vegetables like tomatoes, carrots, cucumbers, turnips, water chestnuts, leafy greens, and the famous nadur on wooden boats, often sharing cigarettes or hookahs. The sweetness of Kashmir’s water influences the taste of its vegetables. Nadur, a porous and fibrous lake vegetable, is an irreplaceable ingredient in traditional Kashmiri cooking and is said to have been discovered in the 15th century by Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin during a shikara ride on Gil Sar lake. A popular legend claims that the yarn threads from Lalla Ded (1320–1392), a Kashmiri mystic saint, transformed into nadur’s fibers after being thrown into Dal Lake. Sun-dried vegetables, known as hokh syun, are consumed when fresh produce is scarce; they are prepared by peeling, chopping, salting, and sun-drying during summer and include dried tomatoes (ruwangun haech), fenugreek leaves (meeth), lotus stem (nadir haech), Iberian knapweed (kretch), shallot leaves (praan), mint (pudna), bottle gourd (al haech), turnips (gogji haech), quince (bamchount haech), collard greens (hoech haak), and spinach (hoech palak). In the Charar Sharief area, dried pears (tang haech) are considered a delicacy. Shallots, known as praan, are a key flavoring ingredient in many Kashmiri dishes, including soups, stews, curries, and kebabs, and were featured in many of Mughal Emperor Akbar’s feasts in the 16th century. Buthoo village is renowned for producing prized organic shallots. Snow Mountain garlic, or Kashmiri garlic, is a rare single-clove variety of Allium sativum with a bright white to creamy-white clove and a strong, pungent flavor without acidity. The Kashmir Valley is the only place in India where asparagus grows, historically cultivated in Pulwama, Budgam, Rajbagh, Tangmarg, and Gulmarg, with current cultivation restricted to Tangmarg and Gulmarg. Sugarcane does not grow in Kashmir; sugar was imported from erstwhile united Punjab up to 1947 and was among the costliest imports. The Dogra government proposed cultivating sugar maple and beetroot sugar, but the plan did not materialize. In the absence of imported sugar, honey was used, with acacia flower honey produced in Tral, Verinag, and other areas, and Sidr honey from Sidr (jujube) trees being considered one of the world’s finest types. Kashmiri apples are known for their juiciness and flavor, with over 1.9 million metric tonnes produced in 2019—more than any other Indian state—and Kashmir accounts for 90% of India’s walnut production. Kashmiri walnuts are nutrient-rich and in demand globally, with giant walnut trees reaching up to 75 feet in Srinagar. Walnut oil was traditionally used for cooking and imparted a sweeter, nuttier flavor. Muhammad Quli Afshar introduced cherries from Kabul during Akbar’s time; the Mishri variety is famous and sweeter than others and is rich in minerals, vitamins, and plant compounds. Other exotic berries include sweet and sour mulberry (tuell and shah-tuell), raspberry (chhanchh), barberry (kaawducchh), and red berry (haapat maewaa). Strawberries (istaber) are harvested in the Gassu area near Srinagar. Orange cultivation began in Urossa village in Uri, where the warmer climate and soil are suitable for the crop. The region’s microclimate supports Mediterranean crops like lemons and olives; Kashmiri lemons are juicier than those from Punjab. A sub-species of wild olives that grows in harsh conditions is used for grafting, producing about 1,000 liters of extra virgin olive oil annually. Kashmiri grapes are cultivated on 500 to 600 hectares, with annual production ranging from 1,100 to 1,500 metric tonnes. Holstein Friesian and Jersey cows were introduced decades ago, producing 4 million liters of milk daily. Organic Kashmiri butter wrapped in Chinar leaves was traditionally common but is now sold only by a few. A traditionally ripened Himalayan cheese called milk chapati or maish krej is consumed in Kashmir. Kashmiri saffron is renowned for its aroma, color, and medicinal value; Pampore saffron has 8.72% crocin content, higher than Iran’s 6.82%, and received a GI tag in May 2020. Shahi zeera (imperial cumin) belongs to the Apiaceae family and was initially found in the jungles of Gurez Valley; its darker seeds are considered superior due to smell, rarity, and shape. Rock salt consumption is traditional in Kashmir, imported from Khewrah in Pakistani Punjab, where it was first discovered by Alexander the Great’s troops in 326 B.C. Pre-independence, it was imported via the Mughal Road (formerly Namak Route); after partition, supply was blocked. It is now consumed by nearly one-fourth of the population. Spring is a season of rejuvenation in Kashmir, with picnics centered around food. The countryside is adorned with almond (badaam), peach (tsunun), cherry (gilaas), and pear (tang) blossoms, and mustard fields bloom in yellow. Apricot (Tser) blossoms are white with pink or reddish tints and grow from late spring to early summer. Beans are spring vegetables; cherries are late spring to summer fruits; coriander (danival) is a cool herb dominant in spring and summer; garlic (rohan) grows in spring and fall; melons (kharbooz) are grown in spring and summer; tender spring haakh is called kaanul. Harvesting of lotus stem (nadur) begins in September. In the evenings, the samovar bubbles, releasing the fragrance of saffron and cardamom. Cookie-shaped kandi kulchas made of flour, butter, sugar, and poppy seeds are passed around to be dipped in tea. Men fish under the shade of chinar trees in Dalgate. Dandelion leaves (haand) are foraged on foot. Paddy is cut with sickles and stacked to dry. Chestnuts are roasted in dying embers. Bulbous garlic and red potatoes grow together. Saffron fields in Pampore bloom in full view. In hilly areas, maize and walnut trees are seen with fruit ready for harvest. In apple-producing areas like Sopore (North Kashmir) and Shopian (South Kashmir), cartons of apples are transported. During long winters, with short days and limited sunlight and electricity, food becomes a central part of daily life. On window sills and terraces, aubergines, cherry tomatoes, gourds, and turnips are sun-dried. The daan (Kashmiri traditional stove) with twin stoves (Chaer) is always ready for long cooking sessions. When roads are blocked by snow, families gather in the kitchen where the flavor of overnight shab deg fills the space. Kohlrabi (monje) is cold-tolerant and continues to grow in winter, with a little frost even helping it. Notable Kashmiri dishes include kababs, which originated from Turkish soldiers grilling meat on open fires and are now cooked with local spices and served with dips. For most Kashmiris, breakfast consists of fresh bread from a local bakery and a cup of noon chai (salt tea), with bread available year-round but its accompaniments varying. Some affordable luxuries include specific baked goods. Unlike most Indian subcontinent dishes where flavors are added during cooking, wazwan flavors are added before cooking by soaking meat in flavored water (osmosis). Wazas are trained for years to master meat cutting and grinding, traditionally mashed with walnut wood. Kashmir produces large quantities of vegetables and forest produce. Native to the Himalayan foothills, Guchhi or kanaguchhi mushrooms (Morchella species) are highly prized internationally, especially in European cuisine, but large-scale cultivation has failed; they are harvested wild and are among the most expensive fungi, costing up to 30,000 INR per kilogram (approximately €330/kg or US$350/kg) as of 2023. Paneer is known as tschaman in Kashmiri and is spiced with a sweet-savory blend including cinnamon, mace, clove, cumin, and ground coriander; ground ginger is a staple due to the scarcity of fresh ginger. The shadowy underbelly of the wazwan, spicy spreads are served free when Kashmiris eat out or pack food. The traditional practice of shadow fishing, known as Tchaayi Gaad in Anchar Lake near Srinagar, involves fishermen breaking ice in the morning, hiding under blankets or straw umbrellas to attract fish, and using harpoons to catch them. Historically, willow thickets along the lake provided shade for fish, easing fishing. Common fish dishes are consumed. Kashmiris eat more rice than people in the Jammu region. In some rural areas, individuals place an egg in a kanger (fire pot), and the scent of the cooking egg signals readiness. Estimates suggest 50 to 60 birds are killed daily in Kashmir’s wetlands; hunted game (shikaar) is not cooked immediately but hung for days (faisander) to make the meat softer and less fibrous. In British India, the markhor (screw horn goat), the world’s largest wild goat, was considered a challenging game species and is locally regarded as the tastiest wild meat. Indian wild boar was introduced by Maharaja Gulab Singh, a Dogra military general, and was a delicacy for Dogras and Sikhs, though its population declined after 1947 in the Muslim-majority region. Game dishes include markhor and wild boar. Kashmiri Pandits, who were vegetarian and avoided onions and tomatoes, were known as Dal Battas (Dal Pandits). Various Kashmiri pickles are consumed. Nomadic Gujjars and Bakerwals move their herds and settlements seasonally. Kashmiris enjoy sugar; common sweetmeats include traditional baked goods. Before 1918, Abdul Ahad Bhat of Ahdoos studied baking with English bakers at Nedou’s hotel in Srinagar, owned by Austro-Swiss Michael Nedou, and later opened the first Kashmiri bakery. Ahdoos specialized in English pastries and added Kashmiri items as India moved toward independence. Mughal Darbar was established on Residency Road in 1984, and Jee Enn, founded by Ghulam Nabi Sofi in 1972, is located nearby. Many owners and staff of these bakeries trained at Ahdoos. The Kashmir Valley is known for its bakery tradition, particularly in qand.

Gujjars and Bakerwals migrate their herds of dairy cattle and their settlements up and down the mountains according to seasonal changes. Kashmiris have a strong affinity for sugar, and common sweetmeats are consumed in the region. Before 1918, Abdul Ahad Bhat from Ahdoos studied baking under English bakers at Nedou's, a hotel in Srinagar owned by Austro-Swiss Michael Nedou, and quickly mastered the craft, eventually starting the first bakery in Kashmir by a local Kashmiri. Ahdoos specialized in English pastries and, as India moved toward independence from British rule, introduced Kashmiri items to its menu. Mughal Darbar was established on Residency Road in 1984, and Jee Enn, founded by Ghulam Nabi Sofi in 1972, is located on a parallel road. Many owners and staff of these bakeries trained at Ahdoos. The Kashmir Valley is renowned for its bakery tradition, particularly the qandarwan, a variety of leavened breads unique to the region and indicative of Central Asian influence. Bakery shops on Dal Lake or in downtown Srinagar are elaborately arranged, selling breads with golden brown crusts topped with sesame and poppy seeds. Traditional Kashmiri breads include various types of leavened loaves. Wazwan, a multi-course meal in Kashmiri cuisine originating in Kashmir, consists mostly of meat-based dishes using lamb, beef, or mutton, with only a few vegetarian options. It is widely popular across the Kashmir region and served internationally at food festivals and reunions. All dishes are prepared according to halal standards; vegetarians enjoy delicacies such as Dum Alve, Nadur (lotus stem), Haakh (collard greens), and Kashmiri vegetarian pulao, which is made with aromatic spices, vegetables, and dried fruits. Kashmiris are heavy tea drinkers and do not use the term "Kashmiri Chai"; instead, they refer to their popular pinkish, salted tea as "noon chai," which is made with black tea, milk, salt, and bicarbonate of soda, with the color resulting from the unique preparation and soda addition. Kashmiri Hindus call it "Sheer Chai," while Muslims refer to it as "Noon Chai" or "Namkeen Chai," both meaning salty tea. Noon chai is a common breakfast drink taken with breads like baqerkhani, brought fresh from Qandur (Kashmiri: کاندر), or from bakers. It is one of the most essential food items in a Kashmiri household and was traditionally served in large samavars, though today samavars are used only on special occasions. Nuts like almonds and pistachios, as well as edible rose petals, are added before serving, and sometimes malai or fresh cream is included to give the tea body and richness. A 2022 University of Kashmir study found that 87% of springs in the valley have excellent to good water quality, and many rural and backward area residents rely on spring water, which they consider the purest due to spiritual ties with shrines. From the purest spring in Kashmir, Kokernag, Bringi Spring Water is known for high alkalinity and balanced mineral content. Babribyol sharbat is a sweetened milk drink made with rose water or Rooh Afza syrup and soaked sweet basil seeds grown locally. Kashmiri lassi (lyaess), made from yoghurt or kefir, is a salty drink prepared by churning buttermilk with a wooden choomph or churner, requiring rhythmic technique so that buttery fats float to the top in a froth and spices and dried mint are properly balanced. This fermented rice water drink is believed to benefit a sluggish liver. A berry juice drink is prepared at home during Ramadan and appears in the 1977 film Arnimaal, where guests sip it during wedding celebrations. The traditional Kashmiri wazwan, featuring slow-cooked meat dishes, pairs well with whisky, and Loire Valley wine Sancerre complements Kashmiri goshtabeh, while a ripe fruity red works well with the full-bodied roghan josh; Montepulciano is recommended as a wine pairing. During Ramadan, Muslims avoid food during the day but enjoy special meals at dusk, with the menu including khajur ka laddoo, babribyol, kulfi, phirin, seemni, fruit chaat, fruit custard, kateer, and noon chai. The scent of slow-cooked mutton is prominent, and despite Srinagar's unpredictability, spirits are high during Eid Mubarak. Eid-ul-Fitr concludes 30 days of Ramadan and is marked by families attending prayers at mosques or Eidgahs, returning home to welcome guests, and serving Kehwa (saffron tea) and chai with bakery items like cakes, cookies, ghee tchot (a tandoor-baked flatbread), pastries, and savory snacks such as chicken and mutton patties. Well-to-do families often prepare select wazwan dishes like kebabs, rista, shami kebabs, and chicken pieces, and serve other delicacies like kanti (stir-fried meat), mutton or chicken tikki with sauces and green chutney (dhaniya chutney), especially when entertaining sons-in-law. Lunch is typically rice-based with a variety of meat dishes, including yakhni, a dish made with fresh curd and mild spices offering a rich yet subtle flavor. The day begins with the Fajr prayer and a breakfast of bakery goods with dodh kehwa (milky green tea). As the festival nears its end, well-to-do families begin placing orders with wazas for the feast, which is prepared at their homes and then sold to customers. Sacrificial animals include Delhi Walla, Merino Cross, Bakerwal, and Kashmiri sheep varieties. Only vegetarian food is provided to devotees; in Batmaloo and surrounding areas, most people turn vegetarian and consume dried turnips (gogji aare), believed to have helped Kashmir survive a famine during Dawood's time. In Pampore, people cook dried vegetables, eggs, cheese, and other food without meat and invite relatives and friends for lunch or dinner to preserve the saint's tradition. In Khanyar and Sarai Bala areas of Srinagar, devotees gather outside shrines where local and non-local businesses sell traditional Kashmiri food, and pious men sing hymns over offerings of dates and sweets. In Anantnag district, people quit eating meat as a sign of respect for a 16th-century mystic, with few butcher shops open during these seven days, and for three-and-a-half days before and after the saint's Urs, radish braised in tamarind is eaten. For Kashmiri Pandits, the prasad at Shivratri puja includes a charger piled with rice, cooked lamb and fish, and a raw fish atop. On the 9th day of ashad, Pandits offer yellow rice cooked with turmeric, a little oil and salt, along with tsarvan (goat's liver). Navreh, the Kashmiri New Year, is incomplete without nadur; it is a celebration of spring in the Northern hemisphere, occurring around the March equinox, often confused with Nowruz. Tibetan exiles in Kashmir, including members of Tibet's small Muslim population, live in Srinagar, mainly near the 18th-century Hari Parbat fort, and run popular momo (beef dumpling) shops and Tibetan restaurants, offering Cantonese chicken, kumloo wonton, and fried pasta stuffed with minced mushrooms. Kashmiri Sikh cuisine has influences from Punjab, including onions and tomatoes, but is flavored with Kashmiri elements such as badyaan (saunf). Many Indian tourists rely on Vaishno Dhabas, which serve all-vegetarian North Indian food. Some Kashmiri cooking techniques include blanching dandelion stalks (haand) four times to remove bitterness, heating food on both top and bottom using slow charcoal heat, braising haakh leaves in water with a wooden spatula to keep them submerged, and using mustard oil for flavor. Much of Kashmiri cooking relies on a fragrant meat stock made from onions and shallots, which is used to poach freshly shaped meatballs (rista and goshtabeh) with cinnamon and black cardamom, then simmered. Whole spices like cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, and bay leaves are fried in oil—too little results in a lifeless dish, too much in bitterness—and hot ghee or mustard oil is poured on top, garnished with fried praan (shallots) paste and saffron extract. Sliced onions are fried until golden brown and then pureed with minimal water. The yoghurt must be fatty and thick, with a pinch of dried mint added at the end. Dishes are enhanced with saffron extract (in rogan josh and rista) or mawal (dried cockscomb flower), and Kashmiri chilli is sometimes added in excess for red color; tomatoes are incorrectly used as a substitute when mawal and rattanjot are unavailable and are not authentic in Kashmiri cooking. Flavors and textures come from slow-cooking spices with ingredients until their juices and fats melt together. Smoking mustard oil is a process called durust, which prepares it for use after cooling. In the shab deg, the cooking vessel is sealed with dough and cooked over a simmering fire through the long winter night. Dum cooking was popularized by Mughal courts in the 16th century. Goshtabeh and rista, two meatball dishes, are rarely found outside the valley due to their unique texture, which is difficult to replicate. The sheep must be freshly slaughtered and the meat pounded before rigor mortis sets, and the meat is folded while beaten to incorporate air and create a light, fluffy texture. The quality of pots is important, according to wosta (ustad) Nazir Ahmed Aram, who emphasizes the right copper content and recommends wood (walnut and apple) for cooking; cooking on gas is not equivalent. Kashmiri cuisine is a blend of influences from Central Asia, Persia, China, and the Indian subcontinent. Food recipes have been passed down across cultures. Kashmiris are gregarious and value sharing, with language and food being central to regional identity. The saying "one who eats properly shall rule the country" reflects this. A wedding tradition involves newlyweds making roti together, with the bride flattening the dough and the groom flipping it. Kashmiris are very particular about taste, and food connoisseurs can identify the waza (chef) who prepared a dish or distinguish a Kashmiri aubergine from others by smell. When filmmaker Vivek Agnihotri proposed a vegetarian wazwan, social media protested, and Gordon Ramsay faced criticism for his Rogan Josh, with Kashmiris stating the meat cut and gravy were incorrect. In Kashmir, food must taste and look good, with an appealing aroma, and success lies in its visual, olfactory, and gustatory appeal. Any event, from receiving a guest to a wedding or circumcision, becomes a celebration of food preparation, serving, and sharing. Delicacies are shared with neighbors, and it is not shameful to ask for food when scents tempt one. Giant dastarkhaans (white sheets) are spread on the floor to serve meals, serving as the center of hospitality, with meals often inviting 100 to 500 people. Since the insurgency and violence, food has become a symbol of life and celebration. Wazas, descendants of Samarkandi cooks, are a significant political group in Srinagar. All dishes are eaten by hand, reflecting an intimate relationship with food; even elderly people consume marrow bones and ear cartilage after meals, with no hesitation. It is considered disrespectful to refuse food or an extra serving, and people go to great lengths to persuade someone to accept more. Kashmiri language contains many food-related idioms. Historically, Kashmiri women packed extra mutton dishes in old newspapers or plastic bags, a practice that later spread to men who carried leftover meat in their traem (wazwan copper dish), evolving into a social movement with elites providing special carry bags. Even leftover rice is not wasted in marriage functions and is served to animals like dogs and cattle. The practice of using carry bags to transport food evolved into a broader movement that gained social acceptance, with even elite groups participating by providing specially designed carry bags for leftover food.
